stories.brief: Edis de Philippe and the founding of the Israeli Opera trace the creation of a major cultural institution and the woman behind it.
storyBeats: Edis de Philippe, an American soprano, arrived in Palestine in 1945 and began building an opera institution there.
She founded the Israel National Opera, creating a company that would become the country’s principal opera institution.
The new company faced a limited local pool of trained opera singers, so it brought in international guest artists to fill major roles.
During the early 1960s, Plácido Domingo and Marta Ornelas were among the singers associated with the company.
By 1958, the company had staged more than 1,000 performances across Israel, showing how quickly it had become a national cultural presence.
As the years passed, the company’s finances worsened and government support remained insufficient for stability.
The Israel National Opera closed in 1982 after several years of financial problems.
Three years later, in 1985, the Council for Arts and Culture created the New Israeli Opera through a partnership between the Cameri Theatre and the Israel Chamber Orchestra.

stories.brief: Galia Lahav represents the history of an Israeli fashion house, from local design work to an international label.
storyBeats: Galia Lahav was established in Tel Aviv in 1984 as a fashion label founded by designer Galia Lahav.
The brand’s core business centered on bridal and eveningwear rather than mass-market clothing.
Over time, the house built a fashion business around couture-style production and presentation.
In January 2017, it became the first Israeli brand accepted by the Chambre Syndicale de la Haute Couture and was shown at Paris Fashion Week.
That recognition positioned the label inside an elite international fashion framework that Israeli brands had not previously entered.
By 2019, the company was represented by 70 stores in 40 countries.
The label became especially associated with bridal customers and celebrity visibility.
Its international growth transformed it from a local Tel Aviv label into a global fashion house.

stories.brief: Early Israeli opera production is an institutional history of performances, audiences, and cultural infrastructure.

sources.title: Party in honor of "La Traviata" production, 40 years ago, 1923-1963

storyBeats: Before statehood, Mordechai Golinkin began building an opera project around the idea of a Jewish national opera in the Land of Israel.
Golinkin formed a Jewish choir and used it to raise money for the future opera project.
The choir toured and gave concerts in the Russian Empire, creating a financial and organizational base before the move to Palestine.
In 1923 Golinkin emigrated to Mandatory Palestine after gathering enough funds to proceed.
On 28 July 1923, the Erez-Israeli Opera opened with Verdi’s La Traviata under Golinkin’s direction.
Because there was no opera house, the first performance took place in a cinema building.
Golinkin had originally wanted to base the company in Jerusalem, but Tel Aviv was chosen because most performers lived there.

The company’s early institutional footprint survives in the National Library’s opera archive and poster holdings, showing that the production line continued to generate records and commemoration material.
A later archival item commemorated the 1923 La Traviata production forty years on, indicating that the premiere remained a reference point in company memory.
The early opera effort became part of the longer institutional history of opera in Israel, which later moved from pre-state experiments to a fuller national opera ecosystem.

translations.en: The start of opera in Israel

stories.brief: Moshe Safdie’s career links Israeli architecture with major public buildings, urban plans, and museum design.

sources.title: Yad Vashem : Moshe Safdie - the architecture of memory
Native stone : the architecture of Moshe Safdie
Global citizen : the architecture of Moshe Safdie

storyBeats: Moshe Safdie was born in Haifa in 1938 and grew up in Mandatory Palestine and then Israel before his family later moved to Canada.
He studied architecture at McGill University, linking his early Israeli background to formal architectural training in North America.
After graduation he apprenticed with Louis I. Kahn in Philadelphia, absorbing a major modernist influence before returning to Montréal.
In 1964 Safdie founded his own firm to realize Habitat ’67, using his thesis as the basis for a real project.
Habitat ’67 became the project that turned him into an internationally recognized architect and defined his social-housing ideas.
Safdie later designed Yad Vashem’s Holocaust History Museum, bringing his architectural language into a major Israeli public memorial project.
The NLI’s literature on Safdie and Yad Vashem frames that commission as a memory-building project rather than a purely formal building exercise.
His work also includes Israeli-facing architectural commentary and scholarship that place him within debates about modern architecture in Israel.
Safdie’s career moved from Israeli birth and identity into a transnational practice, but key Israeli commissions remained central reference points in his reputation.
By the later stages of his career, Safdie was treated as a major architect whose Israeli origins, museum work, and global projects formed a single long arc.

stories.brief: The Ohel Theatre archive points to the history of a workers’ theater company and its role in Hebrew stage culture.

sources.title: The Ohel theatre was founded in 1925 by Moshe Halevy
Toward a balanced history: Ohel, the workers theatre of Eretz Yisrael as a cultural alternative to Habima

storyBeats: Ohel Theatre was founded in 1925 in Tel Aviv as a workers’ theatre linked to the Histadrut labor federation.
Its founder, Moshe Halevy, had left Habima in order to build a theatre for workers and to shape a distinct cultural project.
The company organized itself as a collective, with members combining acting with agricultural or industrial labor.
Its first production adapted stories by I. L. Peretz, setting an early pattern of Hebrew stage work rooted in Jewish literary material.
By 1926 the company hosted the Modern Artists’ exhibition, which the archive history places among the first modern-art shows in Mandatory Palestine.
In 1927 Ohel staged Dayagim, a socialist play about exploitation, showing that the troupe was linking repertoire to labor politics.
A 1934 European tour broadened Ohel’s profile and was followed by successful productions after the company returned to Palestine.
After its return, the troupe produced The Good Soldier Schweik in 1935, one of its better-known successes.
Until 1958 Ohel served as the official theatre of Histadrut, which tied the company to organized labor for more than three decades.
The company entered a later phase under new leadership in the 1960s and then closed in 1969, ending the institutional history preserved in the archive.

stories.brief: The Batsheva archive collection points to the development of modern dance as a major Israeli cultural institution.
storyBeats: Batsheva Dance Company was founded in 1964 in Tel Aviv by Martha Graham and Baroness Batsheva de Rothschild.
From the start, the company trained and performed within the Martha Graham modern-dance framework.
Its early repertory and training environment connected it to the wider American modern-dance current that had begun influencing Israel.
The company quickly developed an international reputation and became a major platform for dancers who later shaped Israeli dance.
Its roster over the years included figures such as Rina Schenfeld, Moshe Efrati, and Sharon Eyal.
In 1975, Batsheva de Rothschild withdrew her funding, forcing the company into a significant institutional transition.
After that withdrawal, the company gradually moved away from the Graham aesthetic that had defined its early years.
During the transition, the repertory increasingly incorporated works by emerging Israeli choreographers.

In 2024, the Batsheva Dance Company archive became digitally accessible through a collaboration involving the company, the Israeli Dance Archive in Beit Ariela, the National Library of Israel, and Harvard’s Judaica collection.

stories.brief: An adult is on the way to visit a friend in another city when the train is delayed and the platform changes twice. At first they think they still have enough time, but the station screen updates again and the connection becomes tight. They call the friend to say they are already at the station and may arrive later than planned. The friend suggests waiting for the next train or taking a bus part of the way, and they compare the options, costs, and how late the visit would become. After a quick check, the person decides to take the slower route because it is more reliable than rushing between platforms. In the end, they arrive later but without stress, and the friend meets them at the station with a coffee.

Talia asks whether Omer saw the delivery driver leave it at the wrong door, and Omer says he noticed the box outside the apartment but did not open it. They check the label together, confirm the name is correct, and notice one item inside may be broken because the package feels loose. Talia wants to know whether she should refuse the delivery or contact the store first, and Omer suggests taking photos before opening it any further. The practical question is how to deal with a damaged parcel without losing the return option. In the end, Talia documents the damage, contacts customer support, and keeps the package until the store replies.

At a small workplace cafeteria, an employee reaches the counter and realizes they do not have cash or a functioning card with them. The cashier has already started the order, so the person checks their phone and asks whether they can pay by transfer instead. A colleague nearby offers to cover it for now, but the employee prefers to send the money immediately so it does not become a hassle later. There is a short confusion because the app needs the exact amount and the cashier has already rounded the bill with a drink upgrade. After a quick clarification, they agree on the final total, the transfer goes through, and the meal is served without delaying the line. In the end, the employee gets lunch, thanks the colleague, and remembers to keep a backup payment method next time.
